# 1 Samuel Chapter 22 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 164r–164v | **Source Images:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/1SA_022_page_001.jpg, 1SA_022_page_002.jpg

---

**1** David left there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and his father's entire household heard, they went down to join him. **2** Everyone who was in distress, everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter of soul gathered around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him.

**3** From there David went to Mizpeh in Moab and said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother come and stay with you until I learn what God will do for me." **4** So he brought them before the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the entire time David was in the stronghold.

**5** But the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not stay in the stronghold. Go into the land of Judah." So David left and went to the forest of Hereth.

**6** Saul heard that David and his men had been discovered. Saul was sitting in Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height, with his spear in his hand, and all his officials were standing around him. **7** Saul said to them, "Listen now, men of Benjamin! Will the son of Jesse give each of you fields and vineyards? Will he appoint all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds? **8** Is that why all of you have conspired against me? No one tells me when my own son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. Not one of you is concerned about me or tells me that my son has incited my servant to ambush me — as is happening right now!"

**9** Then Doeg the Edomite, who was standing with Saul's officials, spoke up: "I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob. **10** Ahimelech inquired of the LORD for him, gave him provisions, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."

**11** The king sent for the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub along with his entire family — the priests at Nob — and all of them came before the king. **12** Saul said, "Listen now, son of Ahitub." He answered, "Here I am, my lord."

**13** Saul said to him, "Why have you conspired against me — you and the son of Jesse — giving him bread and a sword and inquiring of God for him, so that he could rise up against me and lie in wait, as is happening right now?"

**14** Ahimelech answered the king, "Who among all your servants is as faithful as David — the king's own son-in-law, captain of your bodyguard, and honored in your household? **15** Was that the first time I inquired of God for him? Of course not! Let not the king accuse his servant or any member of my family, for your servant knew nothing at all about any of this."

**16** But the king said, "You will die, Ahimelech — you and your father's entire family."

**17** Then the king ordered the guards standing around him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because they too are on David's side. They knew he was fleeing and did not tell me." But the king's servants refused to raise a hand to strike the priests of the LORD.

**18** So the king said to Doeg, "You turn and strike the priests." And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck them down. He killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod that day. **19** He also put Nob, the city of priests, to the sword — men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep — all by the sword.

**20** But one son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David. **21** Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD. **22** David said to Abiathar, "I knew that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would certainly tell Saul. I am responsible for the deaths of your father's entire family. **23** Stay with me. Do not be afraid. The one who seeks your life seeks mine as well. You are safe with me."

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

This chapter narrates one of the darkest episodes in the Saul cycle: the massacre at Nob. The Hebrew text is stark and unflinching. Saul's paranoid rant in vv. 7-8 reveals a man consumed by tribal suspicion — he accuses his own Benjaminite kinsmen of betrayal, wielding patronage (*sadot u-keramim*, "fields and vineyards") as both bribe and weapon.

The phrase *vayisov* ("he turned") used of Doeg in v. 18 carries grim weight: Saul's own soldiers refused to "stretch out their hand" (*lishloach yad*) against the LORD's priests — the same idiom David will later use to refuse striking Saul. Doeg, the Edomite outsider, has no such scruple. His willingness makes him the instrument of sacrilege.

The totality of destruction at Nob — *me'ish ve'ad-ishah, me'olel ve'ad-yoneq* ("from man to woman, from nursing child to infant") — deliberately echoes the *cherem* language of holy war. What Israel was commanded to do to Amalek (and Saul failed to complete in chapter 15), Saul now inflicts on the LORD's own priests. The irony is devastating and deliberate.

David's admission in v. 22, *anokhi sabboti bekhol-nefesh bet avikha* ("I am the one who caused the death of every person in your father's house"), is one of the most morally honest confessions in the Hebrew Bible. He does not deflect blame onto Doeg or Saul.

— PNEUMA
